_readme: Corporate guard pack. ON by default. With git_remote_hosts empty, a push to a remote host is held (refused at the strict guard level, asked about at the standard one) until you add your company's git hosts (for example a GitHub Enterprise host). The workbench guard refuses agent edits it can recognise, but it cannot see every program that writes files, so keep permission prompts on. Edit it by hand or re-run the installer with --git-hosts. Keys are documented in plugins/workbench-core/scripts/guards/rulepacks/corporate.py. Publishing and sharing (npm/pnpm/yarn publish, twine, cargo, docker push, scp/rsync/sftp to a remote host, S3/Azure/GCS uploads, gists, releases, PR approvals, admin merges, comments and GitHub API writes) always asks you first; a copy to a host or bucket listed in upload_hosts is not asked about. guard_level: standard (the default) asks instead of refusing for a push or upload to a host that is not approved and for skipping git hooks, and lets plain browser navigation through; strict refuses them, as 0.3.1 did, and so does a file that cannot be parsed. Everything else (force-push to main, credential files, .env files, public repositories, changes to the guards' own settings) is refused at both levels. production_hosts: hosts where nothing is built or deployed over ssh. protected_db_tables: tables no SQL write may touch (schema.table is fine). Both are empty = no opinion.
_known_limits: The guard reads the commands Claude runs in the shell. It cannot see commands run from inside a program or script (for example Python or Node), so it catches mistakes, not a determined attempt. Your permission settings and your organisation's own controls (for example repository and network policy) are the real boundary.
